item.title: Mike Walker Leads AI‑Powered Cyber Defense and Autonomous Hacking Tournament
item.description:
Mike Walker Leads AI‑Powered Cyber Defense and Autonomous Hacking Tournament

Mike Walker, a research manager at Microsoft Research, is advancing the use of artificial intelligence in cybersecurity. In a Microsoft Research Podcast he discusses his work on autonomous AI systems that discover and patch software vulnerabilities, the first all‑machine hacking tournament, and his perspective on the social role of security rules.

🔍 Overview

  • Walker’s career combines AI, cybersecurity, and large distributed systems.
  • He helped create the first all‑machine hacking tournament, showing how autonomous AI can compete in vulnerability discovery.
  • His work aims to improve how computers are trained to defend against cyberattacks.

🧩 Background

  • DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge (CGC): Walker led the program that proved autonomous AI could find and patch software flaws. CGC marked its 10th anniversary in 2026.
  • Microsoft Research: As a research manager, he leads projects at the intersection of AI, cybersecurity, and large distributed systems.
  • Prior experience: Participation in hacker culture guided his move into next‑generation cyber defense.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Technical focus areas:
    • Cloud‑native memory analysis
    • Automated malware analysis
    • Next‑generation cyber defense technologies
  • Philosophy on security rules:

    “Well, you have to understand the rules if you want to be able to do what you want.” “Rules are a social construct… when a security system asks something of users, you’re asking for their trust. Trust is a precious commodity. When you squander user trust, the security regime falls down.”

  • Core question raised: Are today’s networked systems any safer than they were a decade ago?

💭 Perspectives

  • Walker emphasizes the need to view security rules within their social context rather than applying instant adjudication.
  • He believes understanding the social dynamics of trust is essential for robust cyber defense.

This story was shared in a Microsoft Research Podcast hosted by Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu.

#AI #Cybersecurity #DARPA #MicrosoftResearch

Source: Learn the rules: The hacker mindset - Microsoft Research

item.title: AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training
item.description:
AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training

AWS has released the Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC), a pre-integrated software stack designed to simplify distributed machine learning training. The image is built, tested as a single unit, and maintained by AWS to ensure compatibility across the various libraries required for multi-node workloads.

🔍 Overview

The Ray Train DLC is a PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries layered on top. It includes the full HuggingFace training stack, allowing users to run fine-tuning jobs without building or pushing new images. AWS publishes these images to the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public, where they can be pulled without credentials.

Component Function
CUDA Runtime Provides the foundational environment for GPU acceleration.
PyTorch Compiled against the specific CUDA runtime in the image.
NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library for GPU communication.
EFA Libraries Userspace libraries for the Elastic Fabric Adapter.
AWS OFI NCCL Plugin Connects NCCL to EFA for high-performance networking.
Ray Coordinates the cluster and manages training libraries.

🧩 How it works

Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two distinct roles, both of which use the same tagged image. Whether running on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) via KubeRay or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), the container’s role is determined by the startup command.

  • Ray Head: Coordinates the cluster, tracks state in the global control store, and runs the dashboard and job server.
  • Ray Worker: Supplies GPUs and executes the training processes, connecting to the head’s address at startup.

On Kubernetes, the KubeRay operator adds a RayCluster resource that builds and maintains these groups from a single manifest.

⚙️ Key details

The Ray Train DLC is designed to be configured entirely from outside the image. Users specify instance types, GPU counts, and network transport settings through external configuration files rather than by modifying the container.

  • Compatibility: The image entrypoint automatically enables bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries if the host’s NVIDIA driver is older than the image’s CUDA version.
  • Performance: Collective operations between instances run over EFA automatically as soon as pods request it, as the EFA stack is pre-installed.
  • Testing: AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests.

🚀 Availability

The Ray Train DLC is available in the Amazon ECR repository under the train-ml tag prefix, sharing a repository with Ray Serve and Ray LLM DLCs.

A provided sample demonstrates the DLC’s capabilities by fine-tuning a Qwen2.5-1.5B model using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances.

#AWS #Ray #PyTorch #MachineLearning #Kubernetes

Source: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: FedAlphaEdit Enables Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Knowledge Editing
item.description:
FedAlphaEdit Enables Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Knowledge Editing

Multiple institutions may each hold private knowledge edits and wish to integrate them into a single large language model without sharing raw edit requests. A new paper titled FedAlphaEdit: Null-Space-Aligned Merging for Collaborative Knowledge Editing (submitted on 8 Oct 2026) proposes a solution.

🔍 Overview

  • Null-space‑constrained editing methods such as AlphaEdit guarantee that each update leaves unrelated knowledge intact.
  • Collaborative frameworks such as CollabEdit aggregate edits from multiple clients without data sharing.
  • A naive combination of these two approaches fails structurally; the paper identifies the cause.
  • FedAlphaEdit is introduced to resolve this failure.

🧩 How it works

  • Aligns local editing (AlphaEdit) and server‑side merging (CollabEdit) under a single null‑space principle.
  • Clients share projected statistics rather than raw edit requests.
  • The server provably recovers the result of editing everything in one place under a one‑shot idealization.

⚙️ Key details

  • Described as the first collaborative knowledge editing framework that aligns both local editing and server‑side merging under a null‑space principle for preserving existing knowledge.
  • Empirical results show the method repairs the collapse and brings edit success and preservation close to the level of centralized editing across two architecture families.

💡 Why it matters

  • Allows institutions that cannot share raw edit data—such as hospitals and financial firms—to jointly maintain a shared model.
  • The shared model closely approximates editing all facts in one place, enabling collaborative updates while respecting data privacy.

#FedAlphaEdit #KnowledgeEditing #NullSpace #CollaborativeAI

Source: FedAlphaEdit: Null-Space-Aligned Merging for Collaborative Knowledge Editing
